Cross-track view

Why a 1 km ribbon can shade an 80 km carpet

The gas layer blocks the boom

The boom sweeps along the shield at the aircraft's speed. Inside hydrogen or helium, sound travels faster than that ( times), so the wave cannot form inside the layer. It dies away within it, and most of the boom reflects back up.

What crosses is a slow swell of Pa that rises over ms. People do not hear that as a boom.

Only steep rays reach the ground

Rays that leave the aircraft within about ° of straight down reach the ground. Rays aimed further sideways bend back up in the warmer lower air. From m above, every ray that reaches the ground crosses the shield within ±500 m of the track. The shield edge sits at °.

What leaks is diffraction off the edges

The noise left on the ground comes from the two long edges: weak Pa pulses that arrive s after the main swell. The narrower the shield, the louder they are. That is why width, not gas thickness, sets the result.

Status,

Where it stands

End of phase 1. The acoustics pass a screen: about 55 m of H₂, 1.5–2 km wide at 20 km, meets the proposed 0.11 psf limit at Mach 2, superbooms included. Buildability is open: tethers, hydrogen and failure modes. The economics do not close: owning the plants brings gross benefit/cost to 0.49 against Boomless Cruise (0.87 with a light M2.2 jet) and 1.75 against subsonic, but net of the extra fuel and CO₂ it stays well below 1 against Boomless and negative against subsonic.

"Capture" is the share of each pair's traffic the shield's aircraft carries. Traffic and costs are screening estimates; web figures were checked only at search-summary level. PLdB: Stevens Mark VII perceived level, the standard loudness metric for sonic booms. "Proxy" values apply a 1 ms rise-time smoothing and are the conservative headline used throughout the study.
